fixes.explanation: Right, the statement is false. Paul says, “I am confident that none of this has escaped his notice, because it was not done in a corner.” So he says the very opposite of a hidden corner. In his words, these events were not done in a corner.

Correct. On their way out, the king and the others say to one another, “This man has done nothing worthy of death or imprisonment.” So the statement is false, because they say the opposite. Imprisonment is right there in what they say he has not done anything worthy of.
King Agrippa tells him, “You have permission to speak for yourself.” That's the green light. Paul is the one who gets to speak, friend.
Right on the money. Agrippa gives permission, then Paul stretches out his hand and begins his defense. He's about to speak for himself, and he starts with his hand stretched out.

Paul says it plainly: “…you are acquainted with all the Jewish customs and controversies.” The charges come from the Jews, so a king who knows those customs can follow what Paul is talking about. It's like explaining a work mix-up to a coworker who already knows how your office runs.
Paul says nothing like that in this speech. He says, “…I stand on trial because of my hope in the promise that God made to our fathers…” That's how he states the charge.
Paul asks, “Why would any of you consider it incredible that God raises the dead?” Notice the words “any of you.” That's a bold way to put a question.
Judging is a big Bible theme, but it's not Paul's word here. He asks, “Why would any of you consider it incredible that God raises the dead?” The question is about God raising the dead.

That's not the verb in Paul's question, friend. He asks, “Why would any of you consider it incredible that God raises the dead?” Remembering is nice, but his question is about God raising the dead. And he asks why anyone would call that incredible.

The voice says, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute Me?” Saul was going after the saints, and the voice says it's Him he's persecuting. I think hearing my own name called twice from heaven would stop me in my tracks.
That's not the question. Paul was on his way to Damascus with the authority and commission of the chief priests. The voice asks, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute Me?”

Priest isn't the word Jesus uses. He says Saul is appointed “…as a servant and as a witness…” Saul had been traveling with the authority and commission of the chief priests, but this job comes from Jesus.
Jesus says they may receive “…forgiveness of sins and an inheritance among those sanctified by faith in Me.” So forgiveness and an inheritance sit together in one sentence. That's two gifts, friend.

A new name sounds nice, friend, but it isn't on Jesus' list here. He says they may receive “…forgiveness of sins and an inheritance among those sanctified by faith in Me.” The gift He names alongside forgiveness is an inheritance, shared with those sanctified by faith in Him.

A long life would be nice, friend, but Jesus doesn't mention it in this line. He says they receive “…forgiveness of sins and an inheritance among those sanctified by faith in Me.” The gift He names is an inheritance, and it comes among those who are sanctified by faith in Him.

Journeys aren't what Festus names. He exclaims in a loud voice, “You are insane, Paul! Your great learning is driving you to madness!” He blames Paul's learning, and he does it at the top of his voice.
Paul says the opposite. He tells Agrippa, “I am confident that none of this has escaped his notice, because it was not done in a corner.” So Paul is confident the king has not missed these things.

Agrippa doesn't say that. Paul asks, “King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know you do.” The king answers with a question about becoming a Christian in such a short time (Acts 26:28). Nothing in the text says he gave up on anything.

That's not his wish, friend. Paul says, “I wish to God that not only you but all who hear me this day may become what I am…” He wishes it for all who hear him, not only the king. The only part he leaves out is “…except for these chains.”
They said the opposite. On the way out, they tell one another, “This man has done nothing worthy of death or imprisonment.” That's a pretty good review of Paul from the people who just heard him.

Agrippa tells Festus, “This man could have been released if he had not appealed to Caesar.” Paul had made that appeal himself earlier (Acts 25:11). So the appeal to Caesar is the very thing Agrippa names.
